# 4 Maccabees Chapter 5 — The EMET Bible (Literal)
**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Greek MS (Codex Sinaiticus) | **Section:** Eleazar's First Confrontation with Antiochus

---

**5:1** When the tyrant Antiochus found that his plan was being resisted and that the people held to their law, he commanded his soldiers to seize every Hebrew and force them to eat food forbidden by the law.

**5:2** Anyone who refused was to be tortured on the wheel and put to death.

**5:3** Among the many who were brought in was Eleazar — a Hebrew of priestly descent, learned in the law, advanced in age, and well known to many of the king's retinue for his philosophical reputation.

**5:4** Antiochus saw him and said:

**5:5** Before I begin your torture, old man, I would counsel you to eat the meat and save your life.

**5:6** I respect your age and your gray hair — but I cannot think a man of your evident cultivation to be truly wise when he holds such views.

**5:7** What is it that compels you to practice the Jewish religion? For it deprives you of the pleasure that nature has given us.

**5:8** It seems to me most foolish to refuse harmless pleasures.

**5:9** I think you would be wiser to act as your countrymen who have already adopted our way of life.

**5:10** I therefore urge you to abandon your outdated prejudices and embrace a new perspective.

**5:11** Have compassion on your old age; honor your venerable years.

**5:12** I give you my word: if you eat the pork I will set you free and bestow upon you the highest honors in my service.

**5:13** But if you persist in your old-fashioned Jewish superstitions, I will torture you to make an example of you for others.

**5:14** And even if some invisible guardian watches over your religion, he will surely excuse a transgression committed under compulsion.

**5:15** When he had said all this, the tyrant commanded the instruments of torture to be brought.

**5:16** Eleazar, as though the command had not been given, looked toward heaven, raised his eyes, and asked for permission to speak.

**5:17** Permission being granted, he addressed the assembly in these words:

**5:18** We who have been persuaded to govern our lives by the divine law, O Antiochus, believe in no compulsion more powerful than our obedience to the law.

**5:19** We consider it right in no respect to transgress the law.

**5:20** Even if our law were, as you suppose, not truly divine — and we had wrongly held it to be so — not even then would it be honorable for us to invalidate our reputation for piety.

**5:21** Do not think it is a small thing for us to eat the defiling food.

**5:22** For transgression of the law in small things or great things is equally weighty, since in both cases the law is equally despised.

**5:23** You mock our philosophy as if we did not truly live by it. But in fact it has taught us self-control, so that we master every pleasure and desire; it has trained us in courage so that we endure every pain willingly; it has schooled us in justice so that in all our dealings we give fair treatment to all; and it has instructed us in godliness so that we worship the one God in the manner that truly befits his majesty.

**5:24** Therefore we do not eat defiling food.

**5:25** Since we believe that the law was established by God, we know also that the Creator of the world, moved by compassion, has granted us what is suited to our souls and has forbidden what is harmful to them.

**5:26** The tyrant, hearing these words, as though they were spoken not by a man of wisdom but by an automaton, dismissed them with contempt and commanded the tortures to be applied.
